concept.name: Distributed Tracing

relationships.description: Connects Distributed Tracing to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Distributed tracing reconstructs the end-to-end execution path of a single request as it fans out across microservices, queues, and databases using propagated trace and span IDs.
spark.keyTakeaway: Propagate W3C `traceparent` headers across every sync and async boundary, and pair low head-sampling rates (1%–5%) with tail-based sampling to capture 100% of errors and p99 outliers.

concept.whyItMatters: In a monolith, a stack trace and local profiler tell you why a request took 2 seconds. In a microservice architecture where one API call triggers 15 RPCs, Kafka messages, and cache lookups, local logs are fragmented across dozens of hosts; distributed tracing stitches those hops into a unified causal waterfall so engineers can pinpoint the exact bottleneck or failing service in seconds.
whenToUse: Diagnosing tail-latency spikes (p95/p99) across multi-hop RPCs, database queries, and third-party API calls.
Mapping live service-to-service dependency graphs and identifying unexpected fan-out, N+1 RPC loops, or synchronous blocking.
Correlating intermittent production errors back to the originating request parameters, upstream caller, and exact failing span.
whenNotToUse: Replacing aggregate Prometheus/OpenTelemetry metrics for real-time alerting, SLO burn-rate math, or capacity planning.
Recording full raw request/response payloads or PII for compliance auditing (use structured audit logs instead).
Profiling CPU-bound instruction-level hotspots inside a single process (use continuous eBPF/flamegraph profilers like Pyroscope).
keyPoints: A **Trace** is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of **Spans** sharing a 128-bit `trace_id`; each span has a 64-bit `span_id`, `parent_span_id`, timestamps, attributes, and status.
W3C Trace Context (`traceparent: 00-<trace_id>-<span_id>-<flags>`) is the vendor-neutral standard for HTTP and gRPC header propagation.
Async boundaries (Kafka, SQS, background thread pools) drop context automatically unless producers inject `traceparent` into message headers and consumers extract it into a span link or child span.

Head-based sampling decides whether to record at the ingress gateway (1%–5%), keeping overhead low but missing rare errors; tail-based sampling buffers spans in a collector for 10–30 s and retains 100% of errors and slow traces.
Span attributes should avoid unbounded high-cardinality keys in metric-derived tags, and sensitive PII must be scrubbed at the OpenTelemetry Collector before storage.

examples.title: Pinpointing an N+1 gRPC Fan-Out in Checkout
examples.scenario: A checkout endpoint's p99 latency jumps from 180 ms to 1.4 s after a release, while average CPU across all pods stays below 30%.
examples.outcome: Inspecting a tail-sampled slow trace in Jaeger reveals 42 sequential `PricingService.GetDiscount` child spans (30 ms each) inside a loop instead of a single batched RPC, cutting p99 back to 165 ms once fixed.

examples.title: Tracing Across Kafka Async Consumers
examples.scenario: An order-fulfillment pipeline processes events via Kafka, and engineers lose visibility as soon as `OrderService` publishes to `orders.created`.
examples.outcome: Injecting W3C `traceparent` into Kafka record headers and extracting it in the consumer with `SpanKind.CONSUMER` connects the producer and consumer timelines in Grafana Tempo.

tradeOffs.pro: Head sampling makes a stateless O(1) decision at ingress, requiring zero collector memory and minimal network bandwidth.
tradeOffs.con: At a 1% head-sampling rate, 99% of rare 500 errors and p99 latency spikes are discarded before you even know they failed; tail sampling fixes this at the cost of stateful collector RAM and consistent-hash routing by `trace_id`.

tradeOffs.factor: Rich Span Attributes vs. Ingestion & Storage Cost
tradeOffs.pro: Attaching `tenant_id`, `db.statement`, and `http.route` speeds up root-cause debugging without switching to log search.
tradeOffs.con: Verbose attributes and unaggregated SQL strings inflate OTLP payload sizes (often 1–3 KB per span) and drive up backend storage bills.

tradeOffs.pro: OTel agents/middleware capture HTTP, gRPC, and SQL spans across an entire service in minutes with zero code changes.
tradeOffs.con: Auto-instrumentation misses internal business-logic boundaries, batch item loops, and custom thread-pool handoffs that manual spans illuminate.

failureModes.name: Orphaned Traces Across Async & Thread Boundaries
failureModes.description: A service spawns a background goroutine, CompletableFuture, or Kafka message without copying the active OTel context, splitting one logical request into disconnected root traces.
failureModes.mitigation: Wrap executors with context-propagating decorators (`Context.taskWrapping`) and enforce header injection/extraction in shared messaging client libraries.

failureModes.name: Tail-Sampling Collector OOM
failureModes.description: During a traffic spike, buffering 100% of unsampled spans in the OpenTelemetry Collector for 30 s exhausts memory and drops spans cluster-wide.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a two-tier collector topology with `loadbalancingexporter` (routing by `trace_id`), cap `decision_wait` (e.g., 10 s), and set `num_traces` memory limits.

failureModes.name: Clock Skew Inverting Parent-Child Timelines
failureModes.description: Service B's host clock lags Service A's by 40 ms, making Service B's child span appear to start before Service A's client span.
failureModes.mitigation: Sync host clocks via NTP/Chrony (`< 5 ms` skew) and enable clock-skew adjustment in the tracing UI (Jaeger/Tempo) using client-send/server-receive relationships.

failureModes.name: Instrumentation Overhead & Blocking Exporters
failureModes.description: Configuring a synchronous span exporter on the request thread stalls application handlers whenever the collector is unreachable.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use an asynchronous `BatchSpanProcessor` with bounded queue sizes and drop-on-full semantics so telemetry never degrades application availability.

commonMistakes: Deploying tail-based sampling behind a round-robin load balancer instead of routing by `trace_id`, causing spans from the same trace to land on different collectors.
Logging raw `trace_id` only in errors rather than injecting `trace_id` and `span_id` into every structured JSON log line for trace-to-log correlation.
Leaving 100% head sampling enabled in production, blowing through collector CPU and observability budgets.
Forgetting to propagate `traceparent` across API gateways, reverse proxies (Nginx/Envoy), or serverless queues.
Creating spans inside tight loops (e.g., 10,000 iterations of an in-memory parse), generating massive trace payloads that crash browsers on render.

sections.content:
## The idea

Distributed tracing models a request's journey through a distributed system as a **tree (or DAG) of timed operations called spans**. Every incoming request is assigned a globally unique 128-bit `trace_id` at the edge. Each service hop creates a child **span** with its own 64-bit `span_id`, records `parent_span_id`, measures start/end timestamps, and attaches structured metadata (`http.status_code`, `db.system`, `peer.service`).

For the tree to stay connected, the active trace context must cross process boundaries via **context propagation**—most commonly the **W3C Trace Context** standard (`traceparent` and `tracestate` headers). Once spans complete, an in-process SDK batches and ships them via **OTLP (OpenTelemetry Protocol)** over gRPC (port `4317`) or HTTP (`4318`) to an **OpenTelemetry Collector**, which handles PII redaction, tail-based sampling, and export to backends like Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, or Datadog.

## Concrete walkthrough

Follow a `POST /v1/orders` request through an instrumented e-commerce stack using W3C Trace Context and tail-based sampling:

1. **Edge Context Creation**: The API Gateway receives the request with no `traceparent` header. It generates `trace_id = 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736`, root `span_id = 00f067aa0ba902b7`, and sets `traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01`.
2. **Sync RPC Propagation**: `OrderService` extracts `traceparent`, starts child span `a1b2c3...` (`parent = 00f067aa0ba902b7`), executes a PostgreSQL `INSERT` (captured as a DB child span taking `14 ms`), and calls `InventoryService` over gRPC with the updated `traceparent`.
3. **Async Queue Handoff**: `OrderService` publishes an `OrderCreated` event to Kafka, injecting `traceparent` into the Kafka record headers. A `PaymentWorker` consumes the message `40 ms` later and starts a new span linked to the producer's `span_id`.
4. **Batch Export (OTLP)**: Each service's `BatchSpanProcessor` flushes completed spans asynchronously every `5 s` (or `512` spans) via OTLP/gRPC to a **Tier-1 OTel Collector**.
5. **Trace-ID Routing & Tail Sampling**: Tier-1 hashes `trace_id` to route all spans for `4bf92f...` to the same **Tier-2 Tail-Sampling Collector**. After a `15 s` `decision_wait`, the collector sees `PaymentWorker` returned `status = ERROR`, so it retains and writes the entire 12-span trace to Grafana Tempo.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Sampling strategies: head, tail, and adaptive
sections.content:
## Sampling strategies: head, tail, and adaptive

Capturing 100% of spans in a high-throughput system (e.g., 50,000 req/s × 20 spans/req = 1M spans/sec) is rarely economical: at ~1.5 KB/span, that generates ~1.5 GB/s of telemetry. Sampling controls this cost without blinding engineers:

- **Head-Based Sampling**: The ingress proxy decides at `t=0` (e.g., `TraceIDRatioBased(0.02)` for 2%) and sets the `01` sampled flag in `traceparent`. Every downstream service honors that flag. Simple and stateless, but blind to whether the request will later fail.
- **Tail-Based Sampling**: All services emit 100% of spans to a Tier-1 collector, which routes by `trace_id` to a Tier-2 collector. Tier-2 buffers spans for `decision_wait` (10–30 s) and keeps 100% of traces where `status == ERROR` or `duration > 1000 ms`, plus a 1% baseline of healthy traces.
- **Adaptive Sampling**: Dynamically adjusts per-endpoint sampling rates so high-volume `/health` endpoints sample at `0.01%` while rare `/v1/refund` endpoints sample at `50%`.

sections.eyebrow: 04 / Tracing vs. metrics vs. structured logs
sections.content:
## Tracing vs. metrics vs. structured logs

| Pillar | Primary Question Answered | Cardinality Tolerance | Storage / Cost Profile | Key Correlation Field |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Metrics** | *"Is the system healthy right now?"* (rates, p99, error %) | Low (bounded labels; avoid `user_id`) | Fixed per time-series; cheapest at scale | `service.name`, `http.route` |
| **Distributed Tracing** | *"Where in the call graph did this request slow down or fail?"* | Medium–High (per-span attributes) | Scales with sampled request volume | `trace_id`, `span_id` |
| **Structured Logs** | *"What exact payload, exception, or branch ran in this step?"* | High (arbitrary JSON fields) | Scales with log verbosity | `trace_id`, `span_id` |

## Failure modes

- **Broken Context Across Queues or Thread Pools**: Spawning async tasks without wrapping the active context creates orphaned root traces. *Mitigation*: Standardize on OTel context-propagating thread-pool wrappers and Kafka/SQS interceptor libraries.
- **Collector Memory Exhaustion Under Tail Sampling**: A 10x traffic surge overflows the `decision_wait` buffer, dropping spans silently. *Mitigation*: Enforce `memory_limiter` processors in OTel Collector, cap `num_traces`, and use head sampling (e.g., 10%–20%) upstream if volume exceeds collector RAM.
- **PII Leakage in Span Attributes**: Auto-instrumentation captures raw URL query strings (`?token=...`) or SQL literals containing emails/cards. *Mitigation*: Configure OTel `attributes` / `redaction` processors at the collector to mask regex patterns and drop raw query values.
- **Trace-ID Hashing Mismatch**: Using round-robin load balancing in front of tail-sampling collectors splits a trace's spans across different pods, breaking tail policies. *Mitigation*: Always place a stateless `loadbalancingexporter` (hashing on `traceID`) in front of tail-sampling tiers.

## Log correlation and exemplars

Tracing reaches full diagnostic power when linked bidirectionally with logs and metrics. By configuring your logging framework (e.g., Logback MDC, Python `structlog`, Go `slog`) to read the active OTel span and emit `"trace_id"` and `"span_id"` on every JSON log line, engineers can jump from any error log directly to its full distributed waterfall.

Conversely, **Prometheus Exemplars** attach a concrete `trace_id` to histogram bucket increments (`http_request_duration_seconds_bucket`). When a p99 latency alert fires on a dashboard, clicking the exemplar dot opens an exact slow trace from that spike without searching.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Standardize on **W3C Trace Context** (`traceparent`) across all HTTP gateways, gRPC interceptors, and message-queue headers.
- [ ] Inject `trace_id` and `span_id` into every structured JSON log line for one-click log-to-trace correlation.
- [ ] Use asynchronous `BatchSpanProcessor` exporting over OTLP (`4317`/`4318`) with bounded queues so telemetry backpressure never blocks request threads.
- [ ] If using tail-based sampling, deploy a two-tier OTel Collector topology with `loadbalancingexporter` routing by `traceID`.
- [ ] Scrub PII (auth headers, tokens, raw SQL literals) in the OTel Collector pipeline before persisting spans.

interviewProblems.title: Distributed Tracing
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Distributed Tracing. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Distributed tracing reconstructs the end-to-end execution path of a single request as it fans out across microservices, queues, and databases using propagated trace and span IDs.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: OTel Collector applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Trace Backend.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Trace Backend experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Wrap executors with context-propagating decorators (`Context.taskWrapping`) and enforce header injection/extraction in shared messaging client libraries.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Propagate W3C `traceparent` headers across every sync and async boundary, and pair low head-sampling rates (1%–5%) with tail-based sampling to capture 100% of errors and p99 outliers.
Avoid trap: Deploying tail-based sampling behind a round-robin load balancer instead of routing by `trace_id`, causing spans from the same trace to land on different collectors.
Avoid trap: Logging raw `trace_id` only in errors rather than injecting `trace_id` and `span_id` into every structured JSON log line for trace-to-log correlation.
When to reach for it: Diagnosing tail-latency spikes (p95/p99) across multi-hop RPCs, database queries, and third-party API calls.
When to reach for it: Mapping live service-to-service dependency graphs and identifying unexpected fan-out, N+1 RPC loops, or synchronous blocking.

putItTogether.title: Putting Distributed Tracing Together
putItTogether.summary: Propagate W3C `traceparent` headers across every sync and async boundary, and pair low head-sampling rates (1%–5%) with tail-based sampling to capture 100% of errors and p99 outliers.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Distributed Tracing before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Inspecting a tail-sampled slow trace in Jaeger reveals 42 sequential `PricingService.GetDiscount` child spans (30 ms each) inside a loop instead of a single batched RPC, cutting p99 back to 165 ms once fixed.
